titulo: A digital euro: solution in search of a problem?

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: Few projects in the history of European monetary policy have generated so much paperwork and so little enthusiasm. The European Central Bank has spent several years designing a digital euro, a form of central-bank money that citizens could hold in an electronic wallet and use for everyday payments. Legislators in Brussels are still arguing over the details. Ordinary Europeans, meanwhile, appear largely indifferent. That indifference deserves to be taken seriously, for it raises an uncomfortable question: what exactly is the digital euro for?

Its supporters offer several answers. The first is that cash is in decline. In many euro-area countries, notes and coins account for a shrinking share of transactions, and in some northern countries they have almost disappeared from shops. If the trend continues, the argument goes, citizens will lose their only direct access to public money and will be left entirely dependent on private banks and payment companies. A digital euro would act as a kind of electronic banknote, preserving a public monetary anchor in the digital age.

The second answer concerns sovereignty. A large majority of card payments in Europe are processed by two American networks, and mobile wallets are dominated by American technology giants. European attempts to build a home-grown alternative have repeatedly stalled. For the ECB, this reliance is not merely a commercial matter but a strategic vulnerability: in a more confrontational world, a continent that cannot control its own payment infrastructure exposes itself to pressure from abroad. The rise of dollar-based stablecoins, which some fear could spread among European consumers, has only sharpened these concerns.

Both arguments contain a grain of truth. Neither, however, is quite as compelling as its advocates suggest. Cash is declining, but it has not vanished: in Spain, Italy and Germany a substantial share of people still use it regularly, especially the elderly and those living in rural areas. If the goal is to protect access to public money, the most direct remedy is to protect cash itself, by obliging banks and retailers to keep accepting it, rather than to invent a digital substitute that many of those same people will never use.

The sovereignty argument is stronger, but it confuses the instrument with the problem. What Europe lacks is not a new form of money but a pan-European payment system that is cheap, fast and accepted everywhere. Instant transfers between bank accounts already exist, and several countries have successful national payment apps, such as Bizum in Spain. The challenge is to connect them across borders. That is a task for regulation and private cooperation, and it could probably be accomplished more quickly than launching a central-bank currency that will take years to reach consumers.

There are also genuine risks. The most discussed is financial stability. If households could move their deposits into a digital euro at the click of a button, a crisis could turn a slow bank run into an instant stampede. To prevent this, the ECB proposes a cap on individual holdings, informally put at a few thousand euros. But a cap low enough to protect banks turns the digital euro into little more than a prepaid card, while a cap high enough to be useful threatens the deposits that finance lending to firms and households. Banks, unsurprisingly, have lobbied hard.

Privacy is the second concern. The ECB promises that it will not see who pays whom, and that offline payments would offer a degree of anonymity close to that of cash. Many citizens remain sceptical. Once a public authority builds the pipes through which money flows, the temptation to use them for surveillance, tax enforcement or policy experiments will not disappear simply because officials promise to resist it. Trust in money is fragile, and a digital currency perceived as a monitoring tool could undermine it.

Cost is the third. Banks will have to adapt their systems, retailers will have to accept a new means of payment and the central bank will have to run an infrastructure of enormous complexity. Estimates of the bill for banks alone run into billions of euros. In a region whose lenders are already less profitable than their American rivals, that is no trivial burden, and it will ultimately be passed on to customers in one form or another.

None of this means that the digital euro is a bad idea. A public payment option, carefully designed, could discipline the fees charged by card networks and provide a backstop if private systems fail or are cut off. The mere prospect seems to have encouraged European banks to accelerate their own joint payment projects. Seen in this light, the digital euro may be most useful as a threat: a credible public alternative that pushes the private sector to do better.

But a threat that costs billions and risks destabilising banks must be justified more convincingly than it has been so far. The burden of proof lies with its promoters. They need to explain which concrete problem the digital euro solves that cannot be solved more cheaply by other means, and why Europeans should adopt it when most of them seem perfectly satisfied with the cards and apps they already carry in their pockets.

Until that explanation is forthcoming, the most prudent course would be to proceed slowly: to complete the technical preparation, to protect cash by law and to push hard for an integrated European payment network. If, after that, a gap remains, a digital euro could fill it. Launched in haste and for the wrong reasons, however, it risks becoming an expensive monument to institutional ambition, admired in Frankfurt and ignored everywhere else.
titulo_es: El euro digital: ¿una solución en busca de un problema?
resumen_es: Tribuna de opinión que examina los argumentos a favor del euro digital (declive del efectivo, soberanía en los pagos) y sus riesgos, y aboga por avanzar con prudencia.

ideas_clave.idea: Despite years of work by the ECB, the digital euro arouses little public interest, which casts doubt on its purpose.
Advocates justify it by the decline of cash and by Europe’s dependence on US card networks, tech firms and, potentially, dollar stablecoins.
The author replies that cash is still widely used and that protecting it by law would be a more direct way to preserve access to public money.
On sovereignty, the real gap is an integrated European payment network, which could be built faster by linking existing national systems.
A digital euro could accelerate bank runs; a holding cap either limits its usefulness or endangers bank deposits.
Concerns about surveillance and the high adaptation costs for banks, ultimately paid by customers, add to the doubts.
The project does have merits, chiefly as a credible public alternative that forces private payment providers to improve.
Its promoters must still prove its added value, so the author recommends a cautious approach: protect cash, build a common payment network and only then decide.

resumen_modelo: The author questions the usefulness of the digital euro, a form of central-bank money that the ECB has been designing for years amid widespread public indifference. Its supporters put forward two main arguments: the decline of cash, which could deprive citizens of direct access to public money, and Europe’s strategic dependence on American card networks and technology companies, a concern heightened by the spread of dollar stablecoins. The author finds neither fully convincing. Cash remains widely used in several countries, so the simplest way to safeguard it would be to require its acceptance by law. As for sovereignty, what Europe needs is a cheap, integrated payment system, which could be achieved sooner by connecting existing national solutions. Moreover, the project entails serious risks: it could speed up bank runs, and any limit on holdings would make it either almost useless or a threat to bank deposits. Privacy concerns and the considerable costs for banks, eventually borne by customers, add to these reservations. Nevertheless, the writer acknowledges that a public option could keep card fees in check, act as a safety net and spur the private sector into action. The conclusion is that the burden of proof lies with its promoters and that Europe should proceed cautiously, introducing a digital euro only if a genuine gap persists.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: According to the author, most Europeans are eager to start using a digital euro.
preguntas.cita: Ordinary Europeans, meanwhile, appear largely indifferent.
preguntas.explicacion: El autor dice lo contrario: los ciudadanos parecen en gran medida indiferentes. Esa indiferencia es precisamente el punto de partida de su argumento.

preguntas.pregunta: According to its supporters, what would happen if cash continued to decline?
opciones: Inflation would rise across the euro area
Citizens would depend entirely on private banks and payment firms
The ECB would lose control of interest rates
Shops would stop accepting card payments
respuestas: Citizens would depend entirely on private banks and payment firms
preguntas.cita: will be left entirely dependent on private banks and payment companies
preguntas.explicacion: Los partidarios temen que los ciudadanos pierdan su único acceso directo al dinero público y dependan de entidades privadas. El texto no habla de inflación ni de tipos de interés.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 3 un verbo que signifique «se han estancado, no han avanzado».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a verb meaning ‘failed to make progress’.
preguntas.cita: European attempts to build a home-grown alternative have repeatedly stalled.
preguntas.explicacion: «To stall» significa calarse o estancarse; aquí, que los intentos europeos de crear una alternativa no han prosperado.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The ECB considers dependence on foreign payment networks to be a strategic weakness.
preguntas.cita: this reliance is not merely a commercial matter but a strategic vulnerability
preguntas.explicacion: El texto atribuye al BCE la idea de que la dependencia no es solo comercial sino una vulnerabilidad estratégica.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the author propose as the most direct way to protect access to public money?
opciones: Launching the digital euro as soon as possible
Requiring banks and retailers to keep accepting cash
Subsidising card payments in rural areas
respuestas: Requiring banks and retailers to keep accepting cash
preguntas.cita: the most direct remedy is to protect cash itself, by obliging banks and retailers to keep accepting it
preguntas.explicacion: El autor propone proteger el propio efectivo obligando a aceptarlo. No propone acelerar el euro digital, imprimir billetes nuevos ni subvencionar tarjetas.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The author believes that national payment apps such as Bizum should be banned to make room for the digital euro.
preguntas.cita: The challenge is to connect them across borders.
preguntas.explicacion: El autor cita Bizum como ejemplo de éxito y propone conectar estas aplicaciones entre países, no prohibirlas.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 6 una palabra que signifique «huida en masa, desbandada».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘a sudden panicked rush of many people’.
preguntas.cita: a crisis could turn a slow bank run into an instant stampede
preguntas.explicacion: «Stampede» es una estampida; aquí describe una retirada masiva e instantánea de depósitos.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the dilemma posed by a cap on individual holdings?
opciones: A low cap is illegal under EU law, while a high cap is too expensive
A low cap limits usefulness, while a high cap threatens bank deposits
A low cap favours large banks, while a high cap favours small ones
A low cap increases inflation, while a high cap reduces it
respuestas: A low cap limits usefulness, while a high cap threatens bank deposits
preguntas.cita: a cap high enough to be useful threatens the deposits that finance lending to firms and households
preguntas.explicacion: Un límite bajo convierte el euro digital en poco más que una tarjeta prepago; uno alto amenaza los depósitos. Las otras opciones no aparecen en el texto.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The European Parliament has already voted to guarantee full anonymity for all digital euro payments.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto solo menciona las promesas del BCE sobre privacidad y el escepticismo ciudadano; no dice nada de una votación del Parlamento Europeo.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 9 una palabra que signifique «red de seguridad, respaldo de último recurso».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘a safety net or last resort’.
preguntas.cita: provide a backstop if private systems fail or are cut off
preguntas.explicacion: «Backstop» designa un mecanismo de respaldo que actúa cuando todo lo demás falla.

preguntas.pregunta: In what sense could the digital euro be ‘most useful as a threat’?
opciones: It could be used to sanction foreign banks
It could push private payment providers to improve their services
It could frighten savers into spending more
It could force member states to cut public spending
respuestas: It could push private payment providers to improve their services
preguntas.cita: a credible public alternative that pushes the private sector to do better
preguntas.explicacion: La amenaza es competitiva: una alternativa pública creíble obliga al sector privado a mejorar. No se habla de sanciones ni de política fiscal.

preguntas.pregunta: Why does the author say that the sovereignty argument ‘confuses the instrument with the problem’?
respuestas: Because Europe’s real weakness is the lack of an integrated, cheap and universally accepted payment system, not the lack of a new type of money. That problem could be solved by connecting existing instant-payment solutions through regulation and private cooperation.
preguntas.cita: What Europe lacks is not a new form of money but a pan-European payment system
preguntas.explicacion: El autor distingue entre el problema (falta de una red de pagos europea) y el instrumento propuesto (una nueva forma de dinero), que no sería necesario para resolverlo.

preguntas.pregunta: What course of action does the author recommend, and what does he fear if it is not followed?
respuestas: He recommends proceeding slowly: finishing technical work, protecting cash by law and building an integrated European payment network, and launching a digital euro only if a gap remains. Otherwise, a hasty launch could produce a costly project that nobody uses.
preguntas.cita: the most prudent course would be to proceed slowly
preguntas.explicacion: La conclusión propone prudencia y advierte de que un lanzamiento precipitado daría lugar a un «monumento» caro a la ambición institucional.

tribunal.pregunta: What is the digital euro, and how would it differ from the money in a bank account?
tribunal.pista_es: Definir el euro digital como dinero de banco central frente al dinero bancario privado.
ideas: central-bank money held directly by citizens
bank deposits are a claim on a private bank

tribunal.pregunta: What are the main arguments in favour of the digital euro mentioned in the text?
tribunal.pista_es: Resumir los argumentos del declive del efectivo y de la soberanía.
ideas: dependence on US card networks and tech firms

tribunal.pregunta: Why are banks worried about the project?
tribunal.pista_es: Explicar los riesgos para depósitos, financiación y costes de adaptación.
ideas: outflow of deposits and bank runs

tribunal.pregunta: In Spain, Bizum is very popular. Does that make a digital euro more or less necessary?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar el caso español con la necesidad de una red paneuropea.
ideas: role of the digital euro as a common layer

tribunal.pregunta: Is payment sovereignty a legitimate goal for the European Union? Why?
tribunal.pista_es: Valorar la autonomía estratégica en pagos en un contexto geopolítico tenso.

tribunal.pregunta: How could a digital euro affect the transmission of monetary policy and financial stability?
tribunal.pista_es: Analizar efectos sobre depósitos, crédito y gestión de crisis.

tribunal.pregunta: Do you agree with the author that the digital euro is a solution in search of a problem?
tribunal.pista_es: Tomar una postura argumentada, reconociendo costes y beneficios.
ideas: disagree: strategic insurance in a changing world
importance of public trust and privacy

pánico bancario, retirada masiva de depósitos
